{{Short description|Problem in discrete geometry}}
In [[discrete geometry]], the '''Erdős distinct distances problem''' states that every set of points in the plane has a nearly linear number of distinct distances. It was posed by [[Paul Erdős]] in 1946.<ref name="Erdos1946">{{cite journal
| first=Paul | last=Erdős | author-link=Paul Erdős
| url=http://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1946-03.pdf
| title=On sets of distances of <math>n</math> points
| journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]
| volume=53
| issue=5
| year=1946
| pages=248&ndash;250
| doi=10.2307/2305092
|jstor=2305092}}</ref><ref>{{citation
| first1=Julia | last1=Garibaldi
| first2=Alex | last2=Iosevich
| first3=Steven | last3=Senger
| title=The Erdős Distance Problem
| title-link = The Erdős Distance Problem
| year=2011
| publisher=American Mathematical Society
| place=Providence, RI
| mr=2721878
| isbn=978-0-8218-5281-1
| series=Student Mathematical Library
| volume=56}}</ref> The current best result was achieved by [[Larry Guth]] and [[Nets Katz]] in 2015.<ref name="GuthKatz2015">{{cite journal
| first1=Larry | last1=Guth | authorlink1=Larry Guth
| first2= Nets Hawk | last2=Katz | authorlink2=Nets Katz
| journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]
| doi=10.4007/annals.2015.181.1.2
| title=On the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane
| year=2015
| pages=155–190
| volume=181
| issue=1
| zbl=1310.52019
| arxiv=1011.4105
| mr=3272924}}</ref><ref>[http://terrytao.wordpress.com/2010/11/20/the-guth-katz-bound-on-the-erdos-distance-problem/ The Guth-Katz bound on the Erdős distance problem], a detailed exposition of the proof, by [[Terence Tao]]</ref><ref>[http://gilkalai.wordpress.com/2010/11/20/janos-pach-guth-and-katzs-solution-of-erdos-distinct-distances-problem/ Guth and Katz’s Solution of Erdős’s Distinct Distances Problem], a guest post by [[János Pach]] on [[Gil Kalai]]'s blog</ref> 

Erdős considered this problem as his "most striking contribution to geometry".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Erdős |first=Paul |date=1996 |title=On some of my favourite theorems |url=https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1570291224709357952 |journal=Combinatorics, Paul Erdos is Eighty |volume=0 |pages=97–132}}</ref>

==The conjecture==
Place ''n'' distinct points in a plane. There are <math>\tfrac 12 (n^2-n)</math> distinct pairs between them. Of these pairs, some have the same length, and some have different lengths. The maximum number of different lengths achievable is <math>\tfrac 12 (n^2-n)</math>, using the following points: <math>(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 3), (0, 7), \dots, (0, 2^{n-1}-1)</math>.

The minimum number of different lengths achievable is more difficult to find. Let this number be {{math|''g''(''n'')}}. Equivalently, it is the smallest possible [[cardinality]] of their [[distance set]].

In his 1946 paper, Erdős proved the estimates
:<math>\sqrt{n-3/4}-1/2\leq g(n)\leq c n/\sqrt{\log n}</math>
for some constant <math>c</math>. In big-O notation, <math>g \leq O(n / \sqrt {\log n})</math>. 

The lower bound was given by an easy argument. The upper bound is given by a <math>\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}</math> square grid. For such a grid, there are <math>O( n/\sqrt{\log n})</math> numbers below ''n'' which are sums of two squares, expressed in [[big O notation]]; see [[Landau–Ramanujan constant]].

Erdős conjectured that the upper bound <math>O( n/\sqrt{\log n})</math> is very close to being tight: <math>g(n) = \Omega(n^c)</math> holds for every {{math|''c'' < 1}}, using [[big O notation|big Omega notation]]. More succinctly, <math>g(n) \geq \Omega_*(n)</math>.

He further conjectured that the upper bound is ''exactly'' tight: <math>g(n)= \Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})</math>, and offered a [[Erdős problem|prize]] of $500 for either proving or disproving the conjecture.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Erdős |first=Paul |author-link=Paul Erdős |date=1995 |title=Some of my favourite problems in number theory, combinatorics, and geometry |url=https://www.ime.usp.br/~yoshi/resenhas/abstracts/Erdos.pdf |journal=Resenhas do Instituto de Matemática e Estatística da Universidade de São Paulo |language=en |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=165–186}}</ref>

*{{math|1=''g''(''n'') = &Omega;(''n''<sup>4/5</sup>/log ''n'')}} by Fan Chung, [[Endre Szemerédi]], and [[William T. Trotter]] in 1992,<ref>{{cite journal

== Variants ==

=== Restricted subsets ===
Instead of allowing the ''n'' distinct points to be placed anywhere in a plane, we can additionally require the points to satisfy constraints. In general, the more stringent the constraints are, the larger <math>g</math> gets. 

If we require the points to fall on a single line, then <span style="white-space:nowrap"><math>g_{\text{line}}(n)= n-1</math></span> by setting the points equally spaced. If we require the points to fall on a single circle, then <span style="white-space:nowrap"><math>g_{\text{circle}}(n)= \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math></span> by setting the points equally spaced around the circle. More generally, if we require the points to form a convex polygon, then <span style="white-space:nowrap"><math>g_{\text{convex}}(n)= \lfloor n/2 \rfloor</math></span>. The same, if we require the points to form a strictly convex polygon.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Altman |first=E. |date=February 1963 |title=On a Problem of P. Erdös |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00029890.1963.11990057 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |language=en |volume=70 |issue=2 |pages=148–157 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1963.11990057 |issn=0002-9890|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Altman |first=E. |date=September 1972 |title=Some Theorems on Convex Polygons |url=https://doi.org/10.4153/CMB-1972-060-0 |journal=Canadian Mathematical Bulletin |language=en |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=329–340 |doi=10.4153/CMB-1972-060-0}}</ref>

If we require the points to be in [[general position]], meaning no three points are collinear and no four points are cocircular, then it is an [[open problem]]. Currently the best result is <math>g_{\text{gen}}(n) \geq \Omega(n)</math> and <math>g_{\text{gen}}\leq n2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Erdős |first1=Paul |last2=Füredi |first2=Zoltán |last3=Pach |first3=János |last4=Ruzsa |first4=Imre Z. |date=February 1993 |title=The grid revisted |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0012365X9390155M |journal=Discrete Mathematics |language=en |volume=111 |issue=1–3 |pages=189–196 |doi=10.1016/0012-365X(93)90155-M}}</ref>

If we require the points to be in general position and no four points form a [[parallelogram]], then it is an open problem. Currently the best result is <math>g_{\text{para}}(n) \geq \Omega(n)</math> and <math>g_{\text{para}}\leq O(n^2/ \sqrt{\log n})</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dumitrescu |first=Adrian |date=December 2008 |title=On distinct distances among points in general position and other related problems |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10998-008-8165-4 |journal=Periodica Mathematica Hungarica |language=en |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=165–176 |doi=10.1007/s10998-008-8165-4 |issn=0031-5303|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":0" />

See Section 3 of <ref name=":1">{{cite arXiv |eprint=1406.1949v3 |class=math.CO |first=Adam |last=Sheffer |title=Distinct Distances: Open Problems and Current Bounds |date=2018-07-02}}</ref> for more problems and results of the kind.

=== Higher dimensions ===
Erdős also considered the higher-dimensional variant of the problem: for <math>d\ge 3</math> let <math>g_d(n)</math> denote the minimal possible number of distinct distances among <math>n</math> points in <span style="white-space:nowrap"><math>d</math>-dimensional</span> Euclidean space. He proved that <math>g_d(n)=\Omega(n^{1/d})</math> and <math>g_d(n)=O(n^{2/d})</math> and conjectured that the upper bound is in fact sharp, i.e., <span style="white-space:nowrap"><math>g_d(n)=\Theta(n^{2/d})</math>.</span> József Solymosi and [[Van H. Vu]] obtained the lower bound <span style="white-space:nowrap"><math>g_d(n)=\Omega(n^{2/d - 2/d(d+2)})</math> in 2008.<ref>{{cite journal
| first1=József | last1=Solymosi | author-link1=József Solymosi
| first2=Van H. | last2=Vu | author-link2=Van H. Vu
| title= Near optimal bounds for the Erdős distinct distances problem in high dimensions
| journal=[[Combinatorica]]
| volume=28
| year=2008
| pages=113&ndash;125
| doi=10.1007/s00493-008-2099-1
| mr=2399013
| s2cid=2225458}}</ref></span>

In the other direction, it's known currently that <math>g_3(n) \geq \Omega_*(n^{3/5})</math>, by applying the recursion relation of <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Solymosi |first1=József |last2=Vu |first2=Van H. |date=2008-01-01 |title=Near optimal bounds for the Erdős distinct distances problem in high dimensions |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00493-008-2099-1 |journal=Combinatorica |language=en |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=113–125 |doi=10.1007/s00493-008-2099-1 |issn=1439-6912|url-access=subscription }}</ref> to the result <math>g_2(n) \geq \Omega_*(n)</math> of {{Harvard citation|Guth|Katz|2015}}.<ref name=":1" />

=== Generic norms ===
The same question can be asked for any [[Normed vector space|normed space]]. Given a norm <math>\|\cdot \|</math>, define <math>g_{\|\cdot \|}(n)</math> accordingly. The problem is solved in the ''[[Generic property|generic]]'' case. Specifically, given any integer <math>d\geq 2</math>, for ''almost all'' norms <math>\|\cdot \|</math>,<math display="block"> g_{\|\cdot\|}(n) = (1-o(1)) n</math>That is, the set of norms that violate this condition is [[Meagre set|meagre]] in the set of all norms of <math>\R^d</math>, regarded as a [[metric space]], metrized by the [[Hausdorff distance]] between the norm-unit balls.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alon |first1=Noga |last2=Bucić |first2=Matija |last3=Sauermann |first3=Lisa |date=2025-02-01 |title=Unit and Distinct Distances in Typical Norms |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-025-00698-x |journal=Geometric and Functional Analysis |language=en |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=1–42 |doi=10.1007/s00039-025-00698-x |issn=1420-8970|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
